# Keccak Round Module Behavioral Specification

## 1. Scope

This module implements the state storage and Keccak-f permutation execution for a Keccak-based hashing core. It provides:

- Message absorption by XORing incoming message words into the current state.
- Execution of a complete Keccak-f permutation when triggered.
- Optional side-channel-hardened masked operation using two shares.
- Status and error reporting for completion, state-machine integrity, round-count integrity, and life-cycle escalation.

The module does not perform padding, SHA-3 mode selection, or message authentication.

## 2. Configuration

The module is configured at build time with:

- **State width**: the width of the Keccak state in bits.
- **Message word width**: the width of each incoming message word. The default is 64 bits.
- **Masking enable**: selects between unmasked single-share operation and masked two-share operation.

When masking is disabled, the state is stored as one vector. When masking is enabled, the same logical state is stored as two Boolean shares; the logical state is the XOR of the two shares.

The number of rounds executed per Keccak-f permutation is derived from the state width:

\[
\text{rounds} = 12 + 2 \cdot \log_2(\text{state width} / 25)
\]

For a 1600-bit state, this is 24 rounds.

## 3. Reset and Initialization

On reset, the module shall:

- Clear all state storage to zero.
- Reset the round count to zero.
- Return to its idle condition.
- Deassert the completion indication.
- Deassert all error outputs.

After reset, the module shall be ready to accept message words or a run request.

If the clear input is asserted while the module is idle, all state storage shall be cleared to zero. The module shall remain idle and shall not start a run. Clear is only required to be meaningful while the module is idle.

## 4. Message Absorption

While the module is idle, it shall be ready to accept one message word per cycle.

Each message word is written into a 64-bit position selected by the accompanying address. The module shall XOR the incoming message word into the selected state word. All other state words shall remain unchanged.

Multiple message words can be written in consecutive cycles while the module remains idle. The state therefore accumulates the XOR of all accepted message words.

If masking is enabled, the incoming message word shall be supplied as two share vectors. Each share shall be XORed into the corresponding state share, preserving the logical state value.

A message word presented while the module is not idle shall not update the state. A run request presented while the module is not idle shall have no effect.

The interface protocol assumes that message writes and run requests are not asserted in the same cycle.

## 5. Keccak-f Run Execution

When a run request is accepted while the module is idle, the module shall:

1. Stop accepting message words.
2. Apply the full Keccak-f permutation to the current state.
3. Run the fixed number of rounds derived from the configured state width.
4. Return to idle when the permutation is complete.

The logical state after a completed run shall be identical to the Keccak-f result of the logical state at the start of the run, regardless of whether masking is enabled.

If masking is disabled, the module shall complete one round per cycle.

If masking is enabled, each round shall be processed in multiple sub-steps. The state is updated in two halves rather than as a single whole-state update. The run may take additional cycles if the required fresh randomness is not available, but the resulting logical state shall still match the unmasked Keccak-f result.

At the end of a run:

- The state storage shall contain the final Keccak-f output.
- The completion output shall be asserted for one cycle.
- The round count shall be reset so that the next run starts from the first round.
- The module shall return to idle and be ready for the next message write or run request.

## 6. Masked Operation and Fresh Randomness

When masking is enabled, the module requires fresh random data to remask intermediate values while the Chi step is processed.

The module shall not advance past a masking wait point until it has the required fresh randomness. If randomness is not yet available, it shall hold its current position and continue to indicate that it is not ready. This prevents old randomness from being combined with newly updated state data.

The module may use an early random availability indication. When this indication is present, the module may proceed one cycle before the new random value becomes valid, so that the updated state and the arriving randomness are aligned.

When masking is enabled, the module shall indicate when it needs the next random value. In normal masked operation, one random word is required for each half-state update stage of the round.

When masking is disabled, the module shall not consume random data and shall not require fresh randomness to make progress.

## 7. Outputs and Status

The state output shall continuously reflect the current contents of the state storage.

- In unmasked configuration, the output is a single state vector.
- In masked configuration, the output is two state shares. The logical state is the XOR of the two shares.

The completion output shall be a one-cycle pulse at the end of every full Keccak-f run. It shall not be asserted for individual rounds or while a run is still in progress.

## 8. Error and Escalation Behavior

If the life-cycle escalation input is active, the module shall:

- Stop all normal operation.
- Abandon any run in progress.
- Not generate a completion pulse.
- Not accept message words or new run requests.
- Enter a terminal error condition and assert the control state-machine error output.
- Remain in that condition until reset.

If the control logic detects an illegal or unexpected control state, the module shall also enter the terminal error condition and assert the control state-machine error output.

The round count path includes integrity checking. If the round counter detects an internal mismatch, the module shall assert the round-count error output. This error is reported separately from the control state-machine error.

Error outputs shall be cleared by reset.

## 9. Interface Protocol Summary

For correct operation, the surrounding logic shall follow these rules:

- Message writes are accepted only while the module is idle.
- Run requests are accepted only while the module is idle.
- Message writes and run requests shall not be asserted in the same cycle.
- Clear operations are performed while the module is idle.
- In masked mode, the module must be supplied with fresh randomness when it indicates a need, otherwise it will stall until that randomness is available.

# KMAC Entropy Generation Module: Behavioral Specification

## 1. Purpose

This block provides pseudo-random material for the KMAC/SHA3 subsystem. It is responsible for:

- Obtaining initial entropy from either software-provided seeds or the Entropy Distribution Network (EDN).
- Expanding those seeds into 800-bit pseudo-random blocks used for masking within the Keccak datapath.
- Providing a 64-bit message-mask value derived from the same entropy source.
- Refreshing or replacing entropy under software control, after threshold events, or after configured EDN-related events.
- Reporting errors related to entropy configuration and EDN wait timeouts.
- Providing side-channel protection-oriented status outputs when internal control or counter integrity is lost.

## 2. Initialization and Reset Behavior

On reset, the block must:

- Clear all generated entropy validity state.
- Disable any EDN request.
- Clear error state.
- Return to its reset phase.

After reset, if the software has not yet indicated that entropy is ready, the block must still present a valid random-data output. This output is intended as dummy or placeholder randomness so downstream logic can proceed out of reset without waiting for real entropy. This dummy output is not derived from a software or EDN-configured seed.

When software asserts the entropy-ready indication, the block must:

1. Drop the current dummy random validity.
2. Capture and latch the selected entropy mode.
3. Proceed according to that mode:
   - **Software-seeded mode:** wait for software to supply seed values.
   - **EDN mode:** begin requesting seed values from EDN and arm the wait timer.
   - **Unconfigured or unsupported mode:** report an entropy-mode error and enter the error state.

The entropy mode is latched when the block leaves the reset phase. Software must not change the mode while the block is active; mode changes take effect only after another reset.

## 3. Entropy Modes and Reseeding

The entropy generator is organized so that a full reseed operation uses five fresh 32-bit seed words. Each seed word corresponds to one of five groups inside the generator. Within each group:

- The first sub-generator receives the fresh seed word.
- The second sub-generator receives a permuted copy of the previous state of the first sub-generator.
- The third sub-generator receives a permuted copy of the previous state of the second sub-generator.
- The fourth sub-generator receives a permuted copy of the previous state of the third sub-generator.
- The fifth sub-generator receives a permuted copy of the previous state of the fourth sub-generator.

The permutation used for this forwarding is fixed at configuration time.

This cascaded reseeding behavior applies to both EDN and software-seeded modes. It allows a full internal generator refresh while consuming only five 32-bit words of fresh entropy.

### 3.1. EDN Mode

When operating in EDN mode, the block must:

- Assert an EDN request when a reseed is needed.
- Keep the request active until the reseed sequence completes.
- Accept one 32-bit EDN entropy word at a time.
- Use each accepted word as the fresh seed for the next seed slot.
- Continue requesting EDN words until all five seed slots have been filled.
- After the fifth word is accepted, begin generating a new random output block.

The block enters EDN mode from the reset phase when software indicates entropy-ready with EDN selected.

While in the ready phase, the block must also start an EDN reseed if any of the following conditions occur:

- Software asserts an entropy refresh request.
- A latched hash-count threshold condition is pending.

An entropy refresh request must also clear the hash operation counter.

If random data is consumed while the block is waiting for EDN entropy, the block applies the configured consumption policy to the remaining randomness and continues waiting for the EDN reseed. In fast-process mode, consumption outside the key block does not invalidate the remaining randomness.

### 3.2. Software-Seeded Mode

When operating in software-seeded mode, the block must not request entropy from EDN.

Instead, it must:

- Wait for software to provide five seed words.
- Accept seed-update indications for the five seed registers.
- Require software to provide the seeds in ascending order.
- Use each seed word as the fresh seed for the next seed slot.
- After all five seeds have been provided, load them into the generator and produce a valid random output block.

If software asserts an entropy refresh request in this mode, the block must clear the hash counter but must not perform an EDN reseed.

## 4. Random Data Output Behavior

The block must provide an 800-bit random data output. It must also provide a validity indication and an early or lookahead indication.

The early indication must be asserted when the random data validity is about to be asserted on the following clock cycle.

### 4.1. Normal Consumption Behavior

In normal mode, the block presents a random block as valid.

When the consumer indicates that the current random block has been consumed:

- The first consumption event must be recorded, and the generator should advance, but the current random block remains valid.
- The second consumption event must cause the block to clear the current validity and generate a fresh random block.

This two-consumption behavior supports the two reads needed per Keccak round.

### 4.2. Fast-Process Behavior

Fast-process mode affects how consumption events are handled when the block is not currently processing a key block.

When fast-process mode is enabled and the block is not processing a key block:

- The block must keep the random-data-valid output asserted.
- It must not clear or refresh the random output in response to consumption events.
- The current pseudo-random data is effectively treated as continuous dummy or garbage entropy.

When fast-process mode is enabled and the block is processing a key block, normal consumption behavior applies.

When fast-process mode is disabled, normal consumption behavior applies regardless of key-block processing state.

### 4.3. Message Mask Output

The block must provide a 64-bit message-mask value derived from the same pseudo-random generator output.

When message-masking is enabled:

- The generator must advance every clock cycle.
- The message-mask value and the 800-bit random data output may therefore update every cycle.

When message-masking is disabled:

- The generator must advance only when required by reseeding, generation, or consumption behavior.

## 5. Wait Timer

The block supports a programmable EDN wait timer.

Behavior:

- A non-zero timer limit enables the timer.
- A zero timer limit disables the wait timer, allowing the block to wait for EDN indefinitely.
- The timer is started when the block begins an EDN reseed.
- The timer is scaled by a configured prescaler value.
- If the timer expires before all required EDN words have been received, the block must:
  - Stop waiting for EDN.
  - Cancel the EDN request.
  - Report a wait-timer-expired error.
  - Enter the error state.

## 6. Hash Operation Counter and Threshold

The block must count completed key-block processing operations.

The counter must:

- Increment each time the key-block-processing status transitions from active to inactive.
- Be cleared when software asserts the hash-counter clear request.
- Be cleared when an entropy refresh request is asserted.
- Be cleared when the programmed threshold is reached.

A programmable hash threshold may be supplied. If the threshold value is non-zero and the hash counter reaches or exceeds that threshold:

- The counter must clear.
- The threshold-hit condition must be latched.
- If the block is in EDN mode, the latched threshold-hit condition must trigger an EDN reseed when the block is in the ready phase.
- The threshold-hit condition must be cleared once the corresponding EDN refresh begins.

## 7. Error Reporting and Recovery

The block must report error conditions with an error code and associated information.

### 7.1. EDN Wait Timer Expired

If the EDN wait timer expires, the block must report an error indicating that the EDN response timed out. The associated information may contain the timer state at expiration.

### 7.2. Incorrect Entropy Mode

If software asserts entropy-ready but the selected entropy mode is neither software-seeded mode nor EDN mode, the block must report an error indicating that the entropy mode is invalid. The associated information may contain the mode value supplied by software.

### 7.3. Error State Behavior

When an error has been reported:

- The block must stop requesting new entropy.
- It must not generate fresh entropy.
- It must keep the random-data-valid output asserted so that the currently active hashing operation can complete.
- It must wait for software to acknowledge the error.
- After the error is acknowledged, the block must return to the reset phase.

If software still has entropy-ready asserted and the configuration is valid, the block may reinitialize after acknowledging the error. If the configuration is still invalid, it must report the error again.

## 8. Counter Integrity and Control Integrity

The block must provide a counter-integrity error status. This status must be asserted if any internal counter used for hash counting or reseed sequencing detects a mismatch.

The block must also provide a control-integrity error status. This status must be asserted if the internal control logic enters an unreachable or undefined state. In that case, the block must enter a terminal error state and remain there.

## 9. Life-Cycle Escalation Behavior

When life-cycle escalation is active, the block must:

- Override all normal operational behavior.
- Move unconditionally to the terminal error state.
- Assert the control-integrity error status.

The terminal error state must be sticky; the block must not leave it while life-cycle escalation remains active.

## 10. Summary of Behavioral Requirements

| Condition | Required Behavior |
|---|---|
| After reset, entropy not ready | Present dummy valid random data |
| Entropy-ready with software mode | Wait for five software seed words, then generate random output |
| Entropy-ready with EDN mode | Request and accept five EDN words, then generate random output |
| Entropy-ready with invalid mode | Report incorrect-entropy-mode error |
| Normal random consumption | Keep valid after first consume, refresh after second consume |
| Fast-process mode, no key block | Keep random valid asserted, ignore consumption for refresh |
| Message masking enabled | Advance generator every cycle and provide updated mask |
| EDN wait timer expired | Report wait-timer-expired error and enter error state |
| Hash threshold reached | Clear counter, latch threshold, trigger EDN refresh in EDN mode |
| Software entropy refresh | Clear hash counter; in EDN mode, start EDN reseed |
| Error acknowledged | Return to reset phase |
| Illegal control state | Assert control-integrity error and enter terminal state |
| Life-cycle escalation active | Enter terminal state and assert control-integrity error |
